7502:
I like the idea of Bally/Astrocade, but I think "Bally Astrocade" is too
ingrained to be changed.  Actually, it's one of those nice bits of trivia
for this particular platform that I believe is unique to it, in that it has
a name that refers more to a class of systems than a specific system,
somewhat akin to using "Atari 8-bit" when referring to the entire 8-bit
Atari computer line (my preferred designation and one I've used in my
books), though certainly that uses more system specific names (Atari
400/800, etc.).  In short, I think "Bally Astrocade" should remain as-is
both for the fact that it's now a commonly accepted term and something that
makes the "Bally line" special more or less in all of videogames and
computers.

> There are some options.

1) As you keep a log of changes on the site, it can be used to see what you have added locally but not online yet.

2) Don't know about yours, but my ftp/sftp client checks the sizes of all files and gives back a list of what it thinks you can skip, resume (guessing its incomplete) or over-wright. As such, I can make changes on my local, tell it to upload the entire web directory and then just adjust Resumes in the list to Over-wright. New files are always just uploaded.

This won't help for removing stuff from sections when moved, but can quickly find anything you 'touched' since the last upload.

3) rsync. Don't know if there is a windows version of it, buy like the self checking ftp client, it checks both sets of files. Then it only uploads the 'deltas'. That is, it only uploads what is new or has changed.

Same caveat as the ftp client.

The scans probably got better or worse than the originals because you were scanning in black and white.  If the original text was darker than a certain value, it would come out pure black.  If it was lighter, it would come out pure white.  You can sometimes improve the quality of these scans by adjusting a darkness or threshold value (might be called something different depending on your scanner software).  A grayscale scan might also have been better.  Of course if the original was a photocopy, the damage may have already been done.

7552:
Still looking up FAQ stuff--how deep does the rabbit hole go?

Anyway, we've talked about where Missile Attack (I.C.B.M. Attack modified to use regular controllers) came from before, but now I've looked up some original sources and want to solicit comments, particularly from Brett.

First off, we have the July 1982 Astrobugs newsletter:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/astrobugs/astrobugs_newsletter_july_1982-original.pdf

Brett wrote a column on page 3 mentioning working for Astrocade, and said, "Currently, I am responsible for the new Missile Attack cartridge (#2020)."  I know from Brett's comments to the group that he pitched I.C.B.M. Attack to them, but I didn't think this idea got far enough that it would be given a cartridge number.  Unless of course the Missile Attack Brett referred to in the newsletter was a different game.  Missile Attack (#2020) is seen on some Astrocade materials, but never with a description.

As far as how the Missile Attack that was eventually got released got out, Michael White's catalog has some comments (page 2):

http://www.ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/michael_white_catalog.pdf

"Missile Attack was an entirely different problem.  It was originally released as ICBM Attack with a special hand controller that we can't produce at an affordable price.  Permission was given to change it over to the Bally hand control, but the expert assigned drug his feet and an amateur (me) had to do it!  Control was meant for a track ball or similar device, and it's a bit tricky.  Otherwise, it's a very good version of Missile Command."

And who, you may ask, is the expert dragging his feet?  According to Mike White, it was Don Gladden of New Image.  Message #96:

"I was told to
modify I.C.B.M Attack for the Bally joysticks as Don Gladden [of New Image
software] drug his feet and didn't do it."

Now, I believe New Image did get permission to release some of Astrocade's unfinished carts, such as Bowling and Soccer.  Maybe the same person gave him permission to release Missile Attack.  Whether or not they actually had the right to give this permission is not clear to me at this point.

So, I'm still trying to create a coherent story out of all this.  Maybe something along these lines:

Brett Bilbrey pitches I.C.B.M. Attack to Astrocade, along with the suggestion that a version could be made for the standard controllers.  Before arrangements have been finalized, Astrocade begins advertising this new version as Missile Attack.  Ultimately, they decide to have Brett work on something different, and Spectrecade publishes I.C.B.M. Attack independently.  As Astrocade goes under, Don Gladden gets permission to release their unfinished cartridges.  They mention that they were thinking about updating I.C.B.M. Attack to use regular controllers, and suggest that he make the conversion--even though they don't actually have the rights to the game!  Don Gladden eventually hands the work off to Mike White, who does the conversion and sells a few copies.

It's a compelling story.  Of course, it might not be particularly accurate.  Comments?  I'll also ask Mike White.  I'm thinking up a few questions for him.

Paul

Again, not to belabor the point, but what's wrong with using VHS cassette plastic snap boxes with a printed insert?  You can cut and glue foam to hold the cartridge in place.  Obviously not the ideal, obviously not the most authentic, but lots of homebrews take this approach and it will present a nice boxed game for purchase with minimal cost.  There really isn't the volume in an intended run of roughly 25 to justify the extended costs.  While some of us would certainly pay extra - including me - there are practical limits.  It doesn't have to be perfect or ideal, only good and quality, and I think using VHS plastic snap boxes or some other similar plastic casing (even a lot from a dollar store), would be perfectly fine.

using VHS cassette plastic snap boxes with a printed insert?  You can cut
and glue foam to hold the cartridge in place.  Obviously not the ideal,

are practical limits.  It doesn't have to be perfect or ideal, only good
and quality, and I think using VHS plastic snap boxes or some other similar
plastic casing (even a lot from a dollar store), would be perfectly
fine.

7560:
Lance's response got me thinking: what's wrong with trying to re-produce the original Bally box?  The same exact box would be perfect in a lot of ways:

1) You could buy in bulk, which should result in a cheaper cost.

2) The game manual would be the artwork, just like the original Bally carts.  The manual size would be the template size for any future game releases. 

3) The box could have all the various Bally/Astrocade incarnations (BHLC, BPA, BCS and Astrocade) and artwork (something cool looking), maybe pics of the systems, and on the back of the box you could have a small write up of the system, maybe a recap of what the system was, when it was introduced, etc. etc. and then maybe the system specs of the consoles.  Perfect generic box for Bally home brew games.

4) Add small patch of Velcro or two to the back flap of the box so It stays closed and can be re-opened (like those cardboard DVD sleeves on some Special Edition movies, like Disney's, where you can open the flap). 

I can supply a spare box if someone wants to tear one down for the dimensions, maybe make a template for it?  That could be used to shop around to some printers?  Maybe even a place like Kinko's could do this?  Not sure, never really used them for this kind of thing.  But a box template might help in shopping around for this job.

7567:
To answer your "good enough" question, as a purchaser of way-too-many
homebrews for every conceivable system, the simple answer is, it varies
wildly.  Some, particularly Atari 2600 and ColecoVision often come in nice
full color boxes that look a lot like regular commercial games.  Others,
like for the Vectrex, often come in plastic VHS boxes.  Others still -
particularly disc-based games like for the 3DO, Jaguar CD and Sega CD - use
DVD cases.  A select few use custom (or one-off) cases or boxes.  In all
circumstances, it's "good enough" because that was the chosen method for
distribution.  That's what makes it special.  As long as reasonable effort
is put into printing and assembly - and nothing is half-assed - it will be
the perfect collectible and, in this case, addition to the Astrocade mythos.
Really, the packaging, manual, etc., are the least of the concerns.  The
primary concern is get the game done and out on cartridge.

> First of all, thanks for writing and for your interest. I'll tell you about how I believe things are:

> If I'm nos mistaken, Astrocades' cartridge -the plastic box- measures approximately the same as a cassette tape, which is a size that fits perfectly to the size of the boxes we used for "The Enchanted Crown", which allows to store either a cassette tape or a MSX cartridge, approximately some 11x7 centimeters. To check it I can send you an empty box of "The Crown" for you to check it yourself, there's no inconvenience for me, just send me your post address and I send it to you free of charge.

> You'll see it was printed in offset, laminated and that it has a double width front cover, which has two purposes: it gives more resistance to the cover and allows printing in both sides, which has a more appealing looking when opened. The inconvenience of offset printing is that the printing requires a minimum amount, normally 100. I can check the costs for digital printing, which has a printed result not as good but it works and there should be no minimum amount of units to print. But in this case the unit cost increases.

> For "The Crown" we ordered 150 boxes in offset and it cost us 500 euros, each one 3.33 euros. In this 500 euros it is included handling and the working of the swage machine [this word got me, the original is "troqueladora", I think it is the machine responsible for cutting the boxes]. If we had ordered 300 boxes the cost would raise to 600 euros, 2 euros each unit. I don't know the costs for digital printing but I can guess a maximum price around 8 to 10 euros each box, though it is only a supposition, tomorrow at morning I'm going to ask the prices at the printer and I'll inform you.

> One advantage you have is the cutter [again, the original word is "troquel", I'm supposing it is the cutting layout to produce the boxes outlines in cardboard] is already made and paid, you can use ours and we will not charge you for that. To make a new "cutter" costs around 250 euros, so it is a considerable amount you are going to save.

> There is another alternative, much cheaper but not as "powerful" as "The Crown" boxes which is the Shockware-like packaging. It is a box that fits exactly the cartridge size - I'm including an image - [here, ] and it comes with a detachable "spin" to protect the side of the cartridge. This type of package costs only 1,50 euros each, it is printed in digital format and if you wish I can send you one along with one of "The Enchanted Crown" boxes.

> During previous years I've been working in videogame magazines, I made videogames and I keep doing it, we like to help and cooperate with all those people who ask our help and advice, so you can count on me for everything you need. For example, in the case of the Shockware service I make the design for the labels, boxes and manuals myself for those who can't or doesn't know how to do it, I make it with great satisfaction and for free, so in case you need help with this you can count on me. 7600:
I figured I'd update everyone on the cartridge manual situation, as
there's been some more progress lately.  First, I'll be uploading three
new scans to the FTP server.  First, big thanks to J.C. at atari2600.com
for providing a scan of the Sneaky Snake instructions!  These are no
doubt quite rare.  Then, I've scanned the Astrovision versions of the
instructions for Red Baron/Panzer Attack and Amazing Maze/Tic-Tac-Toe.
Red Baron has some nice WWI-inspired artwork.  Amazing Maze has
different game artwork than the prototype instructions now on-line.

Also, atari2600.com had pictures of a few of Mike White's text
instructions for the prototypes he released.  I'm adding a line to the
instructions typed out for Soccer and Shootout, as this was missing from
the ones typed out on-line.  I'm also typing out the instructions for
Missile Attack.

So, what's left?  Looking at my list from before, I believe it's just
this:

Galaxian-- no instructions, probably only Astrovision-style released
(unless all the instructions said 'Galactic Invasion')

I.C.B.M. Attack -- no instructions, third party

Muncher -- no instructions, sold through Arcadian (unless it didn't
include instructions)

Sea Wolf / Bombardier -- were there instructions with 'Bombardier' on
the cover instead of 'Missile'?  These would probably be from Bally.

I guess my old system had problems I didn't recognize. :(

Other Bonuses 'SPACE INVADERS' labeled cart, Ms.Candy Man cart with manual and colour flyer, 'SOLAR CONQUROR', 'COSMIC RAIDERS' and another 'MUNCHER'.

I apologize for not being clear.  I have many of the astrocade games boxed, and have many doubles.  With a game room of 6500 games, space is everything.  I wanted to make a nice set of clear to read astrologer cassette case inserts for the cartridge based games.  I really could use screenshots of all the games, as that would be one part of the insert.  If anyone knows of a better font to use, then I am all for it.  I am making this in word as that is what I have to work with.    I am more than happy to share my humble attempt at this with all on this forum.

Thank you for asking about artillary duel.  I wish I grew up with the system....but I did not know it existed!  About 9 years ago I found out how wonderful the system was, and my first system(which was a white astrocade by the way), came with artillery duel.  I have been hooked ever since, although I enjoy the colecovision and vic 20 versions as well.  The astrocade controller really works well with this game.  I am missing the ultra rare third party stuff, but other than that, I have all the common and uncommon stuff including most label variants.

7632:
That red is dark enough not to appear pink.  I'm sure you know this but
I'll just cover it briefly for those who zone out when they see this
Verdana font...

A Television set only draws one dot in one color at a time (OK, old
analog TVs do, newer LCD/LED/Plasmas are digital), then move to the
right and draw the next dot's color and brightness.  Once they finish a
line they drop down to the next scanline, and repeat that until a whole
frame is drawn.  This is NOT instantaneous, it takes 1/60th of a second.

MESS makes an image of each timeline, or drops some if Auto- (or a
fixed-rate) Frameskip is on, and that is what is shown.  If one of the
four drawing colors changes during that frame only the dots AFTER the
change take the new color.


Here's the test screenshot from "Fun With Vectors - Ziggy: Update 2" (in
the archive) again.
The background color was changed before and after some system calls to
visually show the time they took to run.  The red stripe was always
there while the fractional movement deltas were added in, but the green
and blue only displayed when the image moved and their routines needed
to be run.  This still took less than the time to draw one frame:

  [Full Size]   Fun With Vectors - Ziggy Timing



Using the larger GhostBusters image instead caused things to take longer
and flicker.
Here are four sequential snapshots taken after a path was cleared in the
full-frame black box by the image moving left-and-right.  The red is
exactly the same size, but the green was still going while the VBLANK
was erasing the image...

  [Full Size]   Fun With Vectors - GhostBusters A

...past where it started on the previous frame!  You can see where the
display scan overtook the erasure, leaving part of the old image
showing.  The amount left would vary on if the image was higher or
lower.  Then the background turned blue while VWRITR started drawing...

  [Full Size]   Fun With Vectors - GhostBusters B

...the new image one pixel to the left.  It had only got half-way done
when the display scan overtook the drawing, so only the top half shows.
It wasn't compleatly drawn until after...

  [Full Size]   Fun With Vectors - GhostBusters C

...the next screen started, when the background is finally turned white
again.

  [Full Size]   Fun With Vectors - GhostBusters D


If Screen Interrupts were set to Mode 0 they would trigger immediatly
once they were re-enabled due to the missed interrupts that were still
pending, causing the red bar to start sooner and making the flicker roll
vertically.

Since this shows them in Mode 1 it waits until a fresh interrupt, and at
least that locks the VECT routine to the same position.

Either way, the long drawing time would cause the "game" to run at
slower than its normal speed.

7649:
Well, as far as I can speak to this...

I don't remember ever doing conversion code to a normal controller. (But heck, I've done lots of things I don't remember doing.)

http://ballyalley.classicgaming.gamespy.com/ballyalley/two_astrocade_pd_programs.html

All I remember is that "Action Graphics" wanted me to work on "Defender" and use the Bally development system. Yuck. That system sucked.

Me, I wanted to program in Z80 and optimize code.

My partners (Mike and Marion) negotiated the deals. Me, I just programmed (for the most part).

I don't know the history of "Missile Attack" so I can't comment on it...

Missile Attack
     Self-Published                            #2020  4k cart  1985.
The available "prototype" of this game is NOT part number 2020; it's a modified
version of "I.C.B.M. Attack" that has been made playable using regular hand
controllers. Thirty-four of these cartridges, modified and manufactured by Mike
White, were sold. In addition, the Astrocade game, "Missile Attack," (as
mentioned in newsletters) as rumored to be "I.C.B.M. Attack" by Spectre, using
Bally hand controls (but Brett Bilbrey, the programmer of "I.C.B.M. Attack"
says this is NOT true). (Michigan Astrobugs Newsletter JUL.82 pg.3, Arcadian
vol.6 pg.99, vol.7 pg.13,46,67,94)

All I can add to this story is that I did not modify it. I think we need to ask Mike White to fill in the history here...

Before arrangements have been finalized, Astrocade begins advertising this new version as Missile Attack. As Astrocade goes under, Don Gladden gets permission to release their unfinished cartridges.  They mention that they were thinking about updating I.C.B.M. Don Gladden eventually hands the work off to Mike White, who does the conversion and sells a few copies.

I'm happy to announce that I've verified the functionality of the last part of the General Video Assembler--the Collector.  Since I don't have source code that actually requires this, I did this by splitting the Logo source code into two parts.  I removed the last couple of lines, output the code, then typed out the last couple of lines, and output this into a separate recording.  Then, the convoluted process began.

1.  Load Pass I.
2.  Load segment 1 into Pass I.
3.  Output segment 1.
4.  Load segment 2 into Pass I.
5.  Output segment 2.
6.  Load Pass II.
7.  Load segment 1 output from Pass I into Pass II.
8.  Output segment 1.
9.  Load segment 2 output from Pass I into Pass II.
10. Output segment 2.
11. Load Collector.
12. Load segment 1 output from Pass II into Collector.
13. Load segment 2 output from Pass II into Collector.
14. Output final object code.

Somehow I got that right on the first try, which is a good thing, since it looks like I'd have had to start over otherwise.  And I thought compiling code at work was a chore!

1. make sure normal AB programs are loading. (I always find that my computer volumes have been changed since last time and unfortunately,

Ok... Slight difference.

That link was a REALLY cool story.  Who is fiddlepaddle?  That's not you, is it Toby?

If you haven't read the original posting by fiddlepaddle, then I'm posting it here:


I went to a small game show yesterday (8 tables). One guy had a mint-looking Astrocade which seemed to work, except the knob on the controller was giving random looking inputs. I just thought it was dirty and a good cleaning would solve the problem, so I paid the guy. As I was about to pack it back up, another vendor ("Larry") sat down and started looking at it. It turns out Larry was one of the other vendors with a table across the room who had a bunch of Astrocade stuff, a pretty complete collection with schematics, lots of games, spare parts, except his console was NOT functioning (my bright idea: 2+2=fun). Larry was once a hardware engineer who worked for Astrocade, Inc.

Anyway, once he started swapping controllers to get it working, and decided there might be a problem with one of the chips inside, I told him I just bought it and I wouldn't mind if he opened it up, so he did. In the next half hour, he had replaced a proprietary D/A chip and got it working and put back together, explaining lots of interesting and useful information about the hardware in the process. I eventually bought all the stuff he brought. The 32 cartridges include the BASIC programming cart and a bunch of cassette games, PACMAN (which he said was unreleased, identified as "PACMAN" in the start up menu, not "MUNCHER" as specified in Wikipedia), and some others I hadn't seen before: "Machine Language Manager", "Artillery Duel V.2.0", "Music Maker", "Sea Devil", "Ms. Candyman". I'm gonna be having some fun this week.

It sure was nice to spend time with people who are genuinely interested in playing the games and finding a good home for a neglected video game system, and not just going for maximum profit. Thank you, Larry!


The Atari Age link that Toby posted has some follow-ups, but this has the whole story.

Adam

Ward asked me to post his response to this "value of a multicart" question.

Adam

Here's his response"

As the guy that made those carts=2C I'd say it's worth
precisely=A0what it's worth to you -- either as a buyer or a seller. If
you do have one=2C and you fully realize how rare it is -- and by that=2C I
mean "next to impossible to replace=2C later" -- then you'll hang onto
it. (I don't even have one=2C any more: my last "for sale" ones all got
sold=3B and Adam has my personal ones -- which I gave to him=2C after my
last Astrocade died around late 2004/early 2005.)
=A0
As with anything out there in the world=2C if you want one=2C and
don't have one already=2C then you have to offer something perceived to
be cooler than the cart itself=2C to whichever of the fewer than 50
individuals on the planet you can locate=2C that has one=2C and will part
with it. (If memory serves=2C I think the "number of prints" that I made
was something like 43=2C total.) And they have to judge how much they
want to keep it=2C versus how easy it's replace-able.
=A0
Some people think my Bally multi-carts are "only worth XYZ
dollars". Some think it's a priceless thing=2C in an artistic or "fun"
sense=3B but=A0that has no fair monetary value=2C per se. It varies by
person. Because each of us value things differently. It's part of our
uniqueness.
=A0
As an interesting aside: an original Van Gogh charcoal sketch was
stolen from it's owner=2C months ago. It had been in that person's
private family collection for 100 years. Pretty much no one outside of
that family even knew it even existed. Museums that specialize in the
works of Van Gogh did not even know it existed. CD-ROMs that said they
contained the complete work of Van Gogh=2C therefore=2C did not have a copy
of it=3B nor was there even a "rumor mill" sort of text suggestion=2C
saying that somewhere out in the world=2C this bit of art even existed.
Apparently=2C from what various news stories have been saying over the
last few weeks=2C the only text that ever referenced that work -- implied
it might exist=2C that is -- was a letter from the artist to someone else
(his brother=2C if memory serves). Which sat in some library or other=2C
for ages: Yale's library=2C I think it was.
=A0
After it's been stolen=2C now people know it exists. So=2C the history
of that one artist has to be rewritten now=2C to say that it does exist=2C
and it always did exist=3B and to try to give the history of who owned it
first=2C and so on and so on. Connecting the artifact back to its creator.
=A0
The punchline of the=A0story is this:=A0it was not only a original
(and previously unknown) work by Van Gogh=2C and one of a kind=2C anywhere
on the planet -- making it "worth=2C" conservatively=2C at least $250=2C000
dollars according to the insurance company that had insured it=2C and
more likely in the range of a million dollars plus=2C according to other
experts ...=A0now that art collectors have another box on a list
somewhere=2C that they'd love to put a checkmark next to ... but despite
all of that hype=2C and sudden "I want it"-ness ... after it had been in
the thief's hands for a while=2C and probably changed hands a few other
times=2C it ended up in a local shop in a small town in New Mexico ... my
hometown of Raton ... and the item was marked as being available for
sale=2C with a price of (wait for it!) only=A0$250 USD.
=A0
Note: it was still there=2C at that local "Antiques and Furniture"
shop=2C when the FBI's Art Theft group arrived to retrieve it. It was
still there=2C because no one bought it=2C for the sum of $250.
=A0
(One reason being: Van Gogh had never signed it. So=2C anyone could
have drawn it. Which implies that it's only "worth" what it is=2C because
that particular artist worked on that item. So=2C if Ward goes on to
become famous or something: the electro-artistic things he worked on=2C
may go up in value=2C accordingly -- at least in the minds of a tiny
group of folks=2C later.)
=A0
My point behind this tale is simple: things have no set value=2C
that everyone agrees on. There is always room for discussion=2C and for
one person valuing something highly=2C while another thinks the same
value is pretty much not worth having=2C even for a pittance.=20
=A0
Things are=A0worth what the buyer and the seller agree they are worth. No m=
ore. No less.
=A0
=A0 -- Ward Shrake --

I've used them for embedded systems development and they are much more useful than a simple serial port/monitor setup.  However, the used in-circuit emulators I've found on ebay didn't include software, were missing parts and now I have a couple boxes in storage that I can't use because the manufacturer doesn't exist any more or they want to sell me a disk with the software for over $1000.

There are some other alternatives such as a ROM emulator.  They are simple and cheap.  The drawback would be that most of these old arcade machines use a lot of ROMs and you'd need to create a board to interface between the ROM emulator and multiple ROM sockets.
They also lack the debugging facilities of an ICE system but they are cheap.

Do you know how much RAM General Video Assembler supports?  I don't mean how much RAM is required to run the assembler, but how much extra RAM can be used.  That is, does it only support 8K, or 16K, or perhaps even more?  How large of a program can acutally be assembled?

Now that I'm extensively programming the 68HC11 in assembly language I find it mind-boggling  that programmers could use assemblers that relied on tape, not only to save programs, but as part of the assembling process.  How long does it take to assemble a program using the General Video Assembler?

It's well-known that programmers from the "old days" routinely programmed directly in machine language either because they didn't know assemblers existed (Jeff Minter programmed his first Vic-20 game before he even KNEW about an assembler), or because the teenagers couldn't afford the assembler, or, as in the case of the Astrocade for several years, their was NO assembler available.

In the case of the Astrocade, programming in machine language was a doubly-tedious process.  First the code had to be created without the aid of an assembler.  Then the code had to be entered using Bally BASIC.  This required numbers to be entered in decimal, but NOT one byte at a time in the range of 0 to 255 (which is what other BASIC languages required).  Bally BASIC required two bytes to be entered at a time because of a quirk in the way that the screen RAM was used.  Two bytes gives a range of 0 to 65,535.  Since Bally BASIC does not accept a number of 32,768 or higher, these large numbers had to be entered as negative.  This meant the range was -32,767 to 32,767.  It must have been pretty tedious work programming in machine code on the Astrocade!

The Machine Language Manager cartridge could have helped with this.  It isn't an assembler, but it does allow hand-assembled code to be entered without the cumbersome method of Bally BASIC.  Paul, or anyone, have you used it>  How much RAM does it support?

I've mentioned before that I'd love to write about this subject in detail, but I probably will never get the time to do this.  If anyone knows of an article about writing in machine code back in the old days, I'd like to read it.  There is a great book on this subject called "Racing the Beam, The Atari Video Computer System" by Nick Montfort and Ian Bogost.  As the title suggests, the book is Atari 2600 specific.  Even this book doesn't cover in detail the tools that were used back then.  What did the programmers have to deal with?  Does anyone know of a title like this?

Adam

The program description should also be updated with the new information.  I suggest something like, "The program instructions say to press any key to get another fortune, but actually the program gives two fortunes in rapid succession, then crashes back to the BASIC prompt when the user presses a key.  This bug has been observed both on the Space Chase master tape, and a commercial tape."

7741:
Hmmm, let's see if I can explain more and then you ask about what does not make sense.
(By the way, I said "Data" chip before, but it is the I/O chip that monitors the inputs. And it seems that the Z80 scans the I/O instead of responding to the interrupt... Hey, it was 30 years ago, I had to go look at the manual...)

(Page 117 in the Nutting manual may help you understand)

The I/O chip (U19) monitors (by use of internal latched registers) the status of input ports (Handle 1-4, and keyboard). There are a few other inputs the I/O chip monitors, but let's not worry about them at the moment. 

The Z80 (U7) reads the state of the input from the I/O chip. Basically the Z80 reads the series of input memory locations (see page 102 of the Nutting manual for Player 1-4 switchs, keypad, and Player 1-4 pots).

OK, so now your question is how does that darn bus work?
This may be what you are having trouble with.

It is a time-division multiplexed bus, meaning that both address and data are communicated on the bus at different times...
Page 123 of the Nutting manual explains how MUXD0-MUXD7 (MXD0-7 on the schematics) via MC1 and MC0 control whether the bus is reading or writing, data or address, to the custom chips.

Once you understand that, you can go to page 128 and see how an "I/O read from port 10H-17H" is done in hardware. Specifically when MC0 and MC1 are being used to write or read address/data.

So, stepping back...
Many things can trigger the Z80 to want to scan the I/O input. The "SENTRY" system subroutine is one such routine. Or countdown timers in the system can 'time out' triggering routines... Or, the programmer can just read the ports directly from his code.

Does this better help answer what I think you are asking?
:-)

I have not looked at my "best of" list again that, but I'm sure that I must have picked "Dog Patch."  When anyone asks about "good" Astrocade games I become a broken record.  My mantra becomes, "Dog Patch.  Dog Patch.  Dog Patch."

The graphics of "Dog Patch" are low quality (even for an Astrocade).  There isn't really much to do in the game at all (you just shoot cans, which, really is just a huge block).  Worst of all, there is no one-player version.  You HAVE to play with two players.  That, also, happens to be the game's strength!  Also, you have to play against a fairly competent player who can manage to keep the can in the air for a while until the bonus score builds higher and higher and you're both fighting for those points that either of you could earn. 

Another problem with "Dig Patch," which isn't its fault, is that it plays terribly in the MESS emulator because it is controlled by the Knob.  There just isn't a good way to emulate that paddle-like device except, well, with a paddle.  So, Jose, if you haven't got the game "Dog Patch," then make it a top priority to get it.  Also, grab a friend who can look past the graphics and just enjoy the gameplay.  You'll both have a smashing good time!

Since Paul mentioned Checkmate, I want to add something about that game that you may not know as a newcomer to the Astrocade.  If you put in the number of players as zero, then the game plays alone at a VERY fast speed (faster then the game ever gets when you play).  It's pretty cool.

There is no modern version of Gorf for whatever reason. It's very difficult
to emulate. Even MAME is not quite right. Gorf has always been one of my
favorites, whether in the arcade, on the ColecoVision or in MAME on my
arcade cabinet. It *is* a mini-game collection of scenes from other
shooters, but it's very colorful and the speech synthesis adds so much
personality to the thing. It's probably the combination of variety, speech
synthesis and unique look that makes the game (and the original arcade
cabinet itself is pretty cool looking as well).

 

There is an unofficial GameBoy Advance homebrew available via the AtariAge
forums. Prior to that, there was Gorf released on CD for the Atari Jaguar (a
recent homebrew), which is very faithful (arguably better than MAME).
Unfortunately for legal reasons, that release had to be pulled from market.
I was lucky to buy my copy before that.

 

I'd put Gorf right up there among my favorite arcade games, along with
Satan's Hollow and Pooyan. I'd love a version for a modern system that is
100% spot-on.
